title: Accuracy, precision and validity in physics

draft.title: Accuracy, precision and validity
card: results are close to the true value. A set of readings can be accurate when their average is near the accepted value.
results agree closely with each other. Precise readings can still be far from the true value.
an investigation is valid when it measures what it set out to measure, and only the independent variable changes the dependent variable. Other variables are controlled.
An investigation can give precise results and still be invalid, for example if a variable that should be controlled is left to change.
draft.remember: Accurate is close to the true value, precise is close together, and valid is measuring what you meant to.

a.q: Four students time a pendulum swing that is known to take 2.00 s. Whose readings are precise but not accurate?
a.why: The readings 2.51, 2.50, 2.52 and 2.51 s agree closely, so they are precise, but they sit well above 2.00 s, so they are not accurate. The readings 2.00, 2.01, 1.99 and 2.00 s are both precise and accurate, which is why that option is tempting.
a.clue: Look for readings that agree with each other but miss 2.00 s.

b.q: Priya tests how the mass of a trolley affects its acceleration down a ramp. She adds mass but also raises the ramp each time. Her timings agree closely. What is the main problem?
opts: The investigation is not valid, as the slope also changed
The timings are not precise, as the mass changed
The investigation is not accurate, as the timings agree
The results are not valid, as the timings agree closely
b.why: Raising the ramp changes a second variable that should be controlled, so the results do not show the effect of mass alone. This makes the investigation invalid. Close agreement of timings shows precision, but precision does not make an investigation valid.
b.clue: Which variable should have been kept the same?

b.best: The investigation is not valid, as the slope also changed
